# Arbitrary simplex containers can have unbounded convexification cost

## Statement and scope

Even allowing nonminimum, jointly chosen enclosing triangles does not give a
bound on their convexification cost by the sum of ordinary fiber depth
deficits. There is an explicit family with three actual planar fibers such
that the summed ordinary deficits are at most 2ε²/9, whereas EVERY choice of
enclosing triangles adds at least ε/16 mixed area after convexification.
This also rules out such a bound for compatible triangle containers chosen
jointly from the outset. All estimates below are uniform over arbitrary
translations, rotations, and shapes of the enclosing triangles.

This is an obstruction to an auxiliary bridge, not a counterexample to (OC).

For a planar convex body K let |K| denote area, and let

    D(K) = max over y∈K of inf over closed halfspaces H containing y
           |K∩H| / |K|.

The maximum exists: for unit u the through-point cap area
|K∩{x:u·x≥u·y}| is jointly continuous in (u,y), by dominated convergence and
zero area of every line. Minimization over the unit circle is continuous in
y, and K is compact. Every triangle has D=Γ=4/9. The ordinary deficit is
δ(K)=|K|[D(K)−Γ], nonnegative by the ordinary Grünbaum inequality.

## 1. An actual three-fiber source

Fix 0<ε≤1/16, put a=1+ε², and define

    T = conv{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)},
    A = {x,y≥0 : ε≤x+y≤1},
    B = ε² T,
    P = {x≤a, y≤a, x+y≥ε}.

The set P is the full-dimensional triangle with vertices
(a,a), (a,ε−a), (ε−a,a). In particular it is bounded. Since
x,y≤1+ε² and x+y≥ε hold for every point of A+B,

    A+B ⊂ P.                                                   (1)

Take the convex body in R×R²

    C = conv( ({0}×A) ∪ ({1}×P/2) ∪ ({2}×B) ).                 (2)

It has projection [0,2] and exactly the three integer fibers

    K0=A,     K1=P/2,     K2=B.                                 (3)

The endpoints follow immediately from extremality of bases 0 and 2. At
base 1, any convex combination using all three bases has equal total
coefficients on the two endpoint bases. Grouping these terms expresses
its continuous coordinate as a convex combination of a point of P/2 and
a point of (A+B)/2; (1) proves the exact middle-fiber assertion. Each fiber
has interior; (2) therefore has ambient interior as well.

Their areas are

    |A|=(1−ε²)/2,     |P/2|=(2a−ε)²/8,     |B|=ε⁴/2.          (4)

The last two fibers are triangles and have zero ordinary deficit. For any
y∈A⊂T, one barycentric coordinate in T is at least 1/3. The associated
through-point cap toward that vertex has T-area at most (4/9)|T|.
Consequently |A|D(A)≤Γ|T| and

    0 ≤ Σj δ(Kj) = δ(A) ≤ Γ(|T|−|A|) = 2ε²/9.                 (5)

This estimate controls the maximum over every candidate of A, rather than
only its centroid. An exact formula for D(A) is not needed.

## 2. A quantitative nested-triangle lemma

**Lemma.** Suppose R is any triangle containing A, and L is any compact
convex set containing both P and R. Then

    (|R|−|A|) + (|L|−|P|)/4 ≥ ε/16.                           (6)

**Proof.** Put Δ=|R|−|A|. If Δ≥ε/16 there is nothing to prove. Hence suppose
Δ<ε/16 and define

    η = 2Δ/(1−ε) < ε/[8(1−ε)] ≤ 2ε/15 < ε/4.                 (7)

For every p=(x,y)∈R, the triangle joining p to the segment
{(0,s):ε≤s≤1} is contained in R. If x<0 its interior is disjoint from A,
and its area is (1−ε)(−x)/2. The same argument using the horizontal edge
and the top edge from (1,0) to (0,1) gives

    x≥−η,     y≥−η,     x+y≤1+2Δ        for every p∈R.          (8)

The top-edge argument is used only when x+y>1; its outside triangle has
area (x+y−1)/2. Thus (8) includes all possible positions of p.

Let q0 be a vertex of R minimizing x+y. Since (ε,0)∈R,

    q0.x+q0.y≤ε,   −η≤q0.x,q0.y≤ε+η.                          (9)

Since (1,0) and (0,1) lie in R, there are vertices q1,q2 with q1.x≥1
and q2.y≥1. These vertices are distinct: if the same vertex had both
properties, (8) would give 2≤1+2Δ<2. They are also different from q0,
because their coordinate sums are at least 1−η>ε. These are consequently
all three vertices of R. Bounds (8) further imply

    |q1.y|≤η,       |q2.x|≤η,       q1.x,q2.y≥1.               (10)

The orientation (q0,q1,q2) is positive. Indeed the two main diagonal
entries of the matrix with columns q1−q0, q2−q0 are at least
1−ε−η, while each off-diagonal entry has absolute value at most ε+2η.
Its determinant is therefore at least

    (1−ε−η)²−(ε+2η)² = (1−2ε−3η)(1+η)>0,                   (11)

using ε≤1/16 and η<ε/4.

Apply the oriented edge inequality for q0q1 to the contained point
(ε,0). It gives, with a positive denominator,

    q0.y ≤ [q1.y/(q1.x−ε)](q0.x−ε).

The analogous inequality for q2q0 at the contained point (0,ε) gives

    q0.x ≤ [q2.x/(q2.y−ε)](q0.y−ε).

Taking absolute-value upper bounds only on their right sides, and using
(9) and (10), yields

    q0.x, q0.y ≤ η(ε+η)/(1−ε),
    q0.x+q0.y ≤ 2η(ε+η)/(1−ε)
                ≤ (5/4)ε² ≤ (5/64)ε < ε/2.                  (12)

The relaxed bound in the second line uses η≤ε/4 and 1/(1−ε)≤2.

Now L contains both q0 and the full lower edge F of P, namely the segment
from (a,ε−a) to (ε−a,a). The triangle conv(F,q0) lies in L and has interior
disjoint from P, because q0.x+q0.y<ε. Its area is

    (2a−ε)[ε−q0.x−q0.y]/2.

Using (12), a≥1, and ε≤1/16, we conclude

    (|L|−|P|)/4
      ≥ (2a−ε)ε/16
      ≥ 31ε/256
      > ε/16.                                                (13)

This proves (6). No support direction or facet of R or L was prescribed,
and L need not itself be a triangle. ∎

## 3. All arbitrary choices of fiber containers are covered

Choose arbitrary enclosing triangles Rj⊃Kj for j=0,1,2; they need not be
minimum containers or satisfy a compatibility condition. Define

    C' = conv ⋃j ({j}×Rj),
    K'j = (C')j.

The endpoint actual fibers are K'0=R0 and K'2=R2. The middle actual fiber
contains both P/2 and (R0+R2)/2. Since 0∈B⊂R2, it in particular contains
R0/2. Thus L=2K'1 is a compact convex set containing P and R0. Applying
(6), and noting that the third fiber excess is nonnegative, proves

    Σz∈Z [ |(C')z| − |Cz| ]
       = (|R0|−|A|) + (|K'1|−|P/2|) + (|R2|−|B|)
       ≥ ε/16.                                               (14)

Both projections remain [0,2]; no additional integer fibers are being
ignored. This is a lower bound on actual fibers after convexification.
In particular it holds if the three enclosing triangles were already
compatible, because then convexification leaves their fibers unchanged.

For any proposed finite constant M≥0, (5) and (14) contradict

    Σz [ |(C')z| − |Cz| ] ≤ M Σj |Kj|[D(Kj)−Γ]

as soon as 0<ε<min{1/16,9/(32M)}; for M=0 any allowed ε works. The argument
does not require dividing by a potentially zero deficit. It proves the
failure for every choice of triangles, including choices optimized
jointly with full knowledge of the source and of ε.

## 4. Extra integer variables

Taking the product of C with [0,1]^(n−1) in additional integer coordinates
repeats each of the three fibers in 2^(n−1) binary layers. At a fixed
binary vertex, a convex combination contributing to that layer can use
only points from that same layer. Therefore (14) applies in every layer,
even when its three triangle containers are chosen differently. The
summed deficit upper bound and the forced added mass both multiply by
2^(n−1). The proposed bridge thus fails for every n≥1 with d=2.

The fact that the small endpoint B has area ε⁴/2 is harmless: it is a
positive, full-dimensional actual fiber, and its triangle deficit is
exactly zero. The obstruction is the contact of the middle triangle with
the tiny removed corner of A, followed by convexity across the integer
bases. It persists for arbitrary enclosing triangles and does not use
minimum-container optimality.

## 5. The obstruction persists with no heavy fiber

The preceding three-fiber source has a large individual fiber. This is not
needed for the obstruction. We now give an actual six-fiber source in
Z²×R² for which EVERY fiber has area strictly below one quarter of the
total mixed area, with a uniform margin.

Use integer coordinates (j,k) and continuous coordinates x∈R². Let C be
the three-dimensional source from (2), with coordinates (j,x). Define

    D = conv( {(j,0,x):(j,x)∈C}
              ∪ {(j,1,x):0≤j≤2, x∈T} ).                      (15)

Its projection is exactly [0,2]×[0,1], and its six actual integer fibers are

    D_(0,0)=A,    D_(1,0)=P/2,    D_(2,0)=B,
    D_(0,1)=T,    D_(1,1)=T,      D_(2,1)=T.                  (16)

Indeed a convex combination with k=0 or k=1 can use only points from that
same layer: those are the two extreme values of the k-coordinate.
Consequently both layer bodies survive unchanged as exposed sections.
This proves every fiber assertion in (16), including the middle bases.
The body D is compact and convex. Both layer bodies have relative
three-dimensional interior, so their hull has four-dimensional interior.

Let W be the total mixed area of D. The three added triangles have zero
ordinary deficit, and hence

    Σ_(j,k) δ(D_(j,k)) = δ(A) ≤ 2ε²/9.                        (17)

Every area in (16) is at most 1/2. For the only possibly less immediate
case, 2a−ε=2+2ε²−ε≤2 since ε≤1/16<1/2, so |P/2|≤1/2.
The upper layer attains area 1/2, and the total is exactly

    W = 3/2 + (1−ε²)/2 + (2+2ε²−ε)²/8 + ε⁴/2
      = 5/2 − ε/2 + ε²[(ε−1/4)²+9/16]
      > 79/32 > 2.                                          (18)

In particular every nonempty fiber satisfies the quantitative strict bound

    |D_(j,k)| ≤ 1/2 < (64/79)(W/4) < W/4.                    (19)

Thus the usual sufficient condition consisting of one fiber with area at
least W/2² is absent, with a margin independent of ε.

Now choose arbitrary enclosing triangles for all six fibers and take their
convex hull at the six integer bases. The projection is still the same
rectangle. Its k=0 section is exactly the convex hull of the three chosen
triangles in that layer, again because k=0 is an exposed extreme value.
The lower-layer added mixed area is at least ε/16 by (14), regardless of
the choices made in the upper layer. All upper-layer excesses are
nonnegative. Therefore the full six-fiber convexification has

    total added mixed area ≥ ε/16,                            (20)

while (17) remains the deficit bound for the source. This establishes the
same unbounded ratio within the class of sources satisfying (19).

For every n≥2, take the product of D with [0,1]^(n−2) in additional integer
coordinates. At each binary vertex, extremality again prevents mixing
with other layers. If W_n denotes the resulting total mixed area, then

    W_n = 2^(n−2) W,
    total ordinary deficits ≤ 2^(n−2)·2ε²/9,
    total added mixed area ≥ 2^(n−2)·ε/16.                    (21)

Every individual fiber still has area at most 1/2, and

    |fiber| < (64/79) W_n/2^n < W_n/2^n.                      (22)

All fibers remain full dimensional. Thus the arbitrary-container bridge
fails, for every n≥2 with d=2, even after excluding the heavy-fiber regime.
